summary: Describes how Network Address Translator devices operate and defines terminology for the different kinds of NAT. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A glossary for the box that lets many computers in a house share one public address, with names for each style of sharing.

questions: what is the difference between basic nat and napt
subtitle: A shared vocabulary for the different kinds of Network Address Translator, and what each one breaks.

tldr.problem: The term Network Address Translator means different things in different contexts, so people talk past each other about what a NAT does and what it costs.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the common terms (address realm, session, ALG), the shared properties of NATs, and the flavors: Basic NAT, NAPT, bi-directional NAT, twice NAT and multihomed NAT, plus Realm Specific IP.
tldr.outcome: It also catalogs the limits: applications that carry addresses in their payload need ALGs, and end-to-end IPsec generally cannot cross a NAT.

today: RFC 2663 is an Informational document and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains a terminology reference for IPv4 NAT, and the text itself states that it does not cover IPv6.

sections.title: What NAT Is and Why It Exists
sections.content:
Network Address Translation maps IP addresses from one address realm to another to give hosts transparent routing. Traditionally a NAT device connects an isolated realm using private, unregistered addresses to an external realm with globally unique, registered ones. This document is limited to IPv4.

All NATs share three traits: transparent address assignment, transparent routing through address translation, and translation of ICMP error packet payloads. A NAT modifies addresses en route and keeps state so that datagrams of a session reach the right end node in either realm.

This only works when applications do not use IP addresses as part of the protocol itself. Otherwise the NAT must be paired with an application level gateway (ALG), an application-specific translation agent. The RFC describes terminology; it does not describe individual NAT variations or say where NAT should be deployed.
sections.eli5: When one building has only one public address but many rooms, a helper rewrites the address on each letter so the replies find the right room.

sections.title: Sessions, Ports and Private Space
sections.content:
NAT translation is session based, where a session is the set of traffic managed as a unit. TCP and UDP sessions are identified by source address, source port, target address and target port. ICMP query sessions use source address, ICMP query ID and target address. Other sessions use source address, target address and IP protocol. The direction of a session is set by its first packet.

A TCP session starts with a packet having SYN set and ACK clear. For UDP and others there is no certain way to detect a start or an end, so heuristics are used and session timeouts must be configurable. A TCP session can be treated as ended 4 minutes after FINs are acknowledged or an RST is seen, following the TIME-WAIT idea in RFC 793.

Private networks typically use the blocks IANA set aside in RFC 1918: 10/8, 172.16/12 and 192.168/16. Organizations using them must renumber or enable NAT to talk to each other or to the public Internet.
sections.eli5: The helper has to remember each conversation so it can pass replies back. Knowing when a conversation is over is surprisingly hard, so it waits a while to be safe.

sections.title: The Flavors of NAT
sections.content:
The RFC uses one base model: Host-A in a private realm behind a NAT router, and Host-X in an external realm.

  • Traditional (outbound) NAT. Sessions are outbound only. Basic NAT translates the source address (and related checksums) using a block of external addresses. NAPT also translates TCP/UDP ports or ICMP query IDs, so many private hosts share a single external address.
  • Bi-directional NAT. Sessions can start from either side. It needs a DNS-ALG to translate addresses in DNS queries and responses.
  • Twice NAT. Both source and destination are translated. It is for when private and external realms have colliding addresses. A DNS-ALG hands the internal host a locally routable stand-in address for the external host.
  • Multihomed NAT. Several NAT boxes or links give fail-safe backup, but backup NATs must exchange state, which is simpler with static maps.

Translation has three phases: address binding, address lookup and translation, and address unbinding. Binding may be static (a fixed one-to-one mapping) or dynamic (assigned per session and freed when the last session ends).
sections.eli5: Some helpers only let people inside call out, some let outsiders call in, and some have to rewrite both the sender and the receiver because two places have the same address.

sections.title: Realm Specific IP and Tunnels
sections.content:
Realm Specific IP (RSIP) is a different approach: a realm-aware host in the private realm adopts an address from the external realm itself, so end-to-end packets need no translation. An RSIP server sits in both realms and helps route those packets.

  • RSA-IP clients adopt an external address. Their packets cross the private realm in a tunnel, either translated by an en-route NAT on the outer header or through a tunnel to the border router.
  • RSAP-IP clients adopt an (external address, transport identifier) tuple, so several hosts share one external address, limited to TCP, UDP and ICMP sessions.

The RFC also covers private networks joined by tunnels. Translation can be used on a VPN link, and a backbone-partitioned private network can avoid translation entirely by encapsulating packets between NAT boxes, each reserving a global address for tunneling.
sections.eli5: Instead of a receptionist rewriting letters, some people borrow a proper outside address and send their letters inside an envelope, so nobody needs to rewrite anything.

sections.title: What NAT Breaks
sections.content:
NATs only touch IP, TCP, UDP and ICMP headers and ICMP error messages, so they are transparent to many applications. There are two main trouble spots: payloads that contain IP addresses, and end-to-end security.

  • FTP. The PORT command and PASV response carry an address and port in ASCII. An FTP ALG must rewrite them, and since the text length can change (for example 18 versus 20 characters), TCP sequence and acknowledgement numbers may need correcting for the rest of the connection.
  • Other applications. SNMP carries addresses in payloads, and H.323 uses control sessions to set up follow-on sessions, which need ALGs.
  • IPsec. AH and ESP integrity checks cover the transport checksum, so a rewritten address makes packets fail either the integrity check or the checksum. Application-layer security such as TLS, SSL and ssh works if it does not depend on addresses. IPsec tunnel mode ESP can work with RSIP.
  • Secure DNS. A DNS-ALG that changes addresses (as in twice NAT) breaks signature verification.

Other limits listed are harder debugging, since one global address may map to different hosts over time, awkward fragmented FTP control packets, and the compute cost of touching every packet.
sections.eli5: If a letter has the return address written inside it as well as on the envelope, the helper must open and fix the letter too. And sealed letters that include the address cannot be fixed at all.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Many people see traditional NAT as a one-way filter that blocks sessions from outside, and dynamic assignment makes it harder to point at a specific host. NAT is often combined with ALGs and firewalls. But ALGs outside a trusted boundary could snoop on user payloads, and apart from RSIP, end-to-end network-level IPsec cannot be had with a NAT in the path. Tunnel mode IPsec works if the NAT router is the tunnel end point.

The RFC adds three specific issues. UDP sessions are inherently unsafe because replies may come from a different address, so partial matching of inbound packets can be a compromise. Multicast sessions have a similar weakness. And NAT devices are Internet hosts, so they can be attacked with SYN floods and ping floods and should be protected like servers.
sections.eli5: The helper does hide who is inside, which feels safe, but it cannot stop every trick, and the helper itself can be bothered or fooled like anyone else.
